newsitem.title: ITALY: Italians count cost of budget, opposition furious.
newsitem.headline: Italians count cost of budget, opposition furious.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi's 1997 budget drew praise from abroad and protests from the opposition on Sunday as Italians counted the cost of measures designed to propel them into European monetary union.
Newspapers ran headlines reckoning the plans announced on Friday would cost the average family one million lire ($660) a year and said Italians could look forward to a bleak Christmas.

Centre-right leader Silvio Berlusconi led a chorus of opposition complaint at the tax hikes contained in the package, which will cut 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's deficit, and promised to unveil a counter-budget on Thursday.
Business leaders called for an immediate cut in interest rates and worried that the government had not yet spelled out the details of a one-off "Euro tax".

But the package got an initial thumbs up from German Finance Minister Theo Waigel at an International Monetary Fund meeting in Washington. Newspapers quoted him praising it as the "most important thing to happen in Italy in the last few months".
A wave of Euro-optimism has propelled Italian bond markets and the lira in recent days on hopes the budget will enable Italy to qualify for a single currency planned for 1999.

Italian Economy Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi also indicated support from IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus. Ciampi quoted him as saying that Italian interest rates could fall if the government continued its current fiscal correction.
Prodi said he, too, hoped the Bank of Italy would soon cut rates as a prelude to the lira rejoining Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism as soon as possible.
He admitted he would have preferred fewer taxes but described the package as "the price of Europe" and said Italy was ready to pay its bill.

But Berlusconi said Prodi had lost all credibility because his centre-left government bowed to pressure from the hard-left Communist Refoundation party not to cut pensions and healthcare benefits and raised taxes instead.
"It will be a disastrous budget that we will oppose vehemently," Berlusconi told La Stampa.
"In parliament, next Thursday, we will do our own counter-budget...It will be inspired by what we've been saying for two years. More cuts and no new taxes."

The government said the heart of the budget was worth 37.5 trillion lire ($24.7 billion), with 25 trillion lire ($16.4 billion) coming from planned spending cuts and 12.5 trillion ($8.2 billion) from fresh revenues.

In addition, the government intends to raise 13 trillion lire from a special Euro tax and 12 trillion lire from so far unspecified "treasury operations". Both measures are due to be fully elaborated before the end of the year.

Berlusconi, who called the budget a "pitch black tunnel", said the measures gave Italians "even more incentive to elude or evade" paying taxes and forecast it would spur secessionary tensions in the rich, industrial north.
"A budget like this will do nothing but accelerate the crisis of the country, split the country," agreed Umberto Bossi, leader of the separatist Northern League party.
Sergio Bille, chairman of trade body Confcommercio, told La Stampa the budget would have "enormous negative effects" and would lead to lower growth that would hurt employment.
Carlo Callieri, vice president of employers' association Confindustria, said the success of the budget depended on the Bank of Italy cutting interest rates soon.
The Bank cut its discount rate to 8.25 percent from nine percent in July after keeping it unchanged for more than a year.
